question: Which statement best describes Server vs client components?
options: In an RSC framework every component is a server component by default: it runs only on the server, ships no JavaScript, and can fetch data directly. Client components are the opt-in exception, declared with 'use client', and are the only ones that can hold state, run effects, attach event handlers, or touch browser APIs. The mental split is data/composition on the server, interaction on the client.

Props passed from a server component to a client component must be serializable, because they travel inside the RSC payload — so strings, numbers, booleans, plain objects, arrays, and JSX are fine, but functions (event handlers), class instances, and Dates-as-behavior are not. This is why you cannot hand a client island an onClick callback from the server; the handler must live inside the client component, or you use a Server Action for server logic.

Server components can be async and await data directly from databases, the filesystem, or internal APIs, eliminating client-side useEffect fetch waterfalls and loading flashes. Because the fetching code never reaches the browser, you can use heavy server-only libraries and secrets safely. Fetch where the data is used and pass already-resolved, serializable data down to client islands as props.

Adding 'use client' to the top of a module marks it — and every module it imports — as part of the client bundle. It does NOT mean 'render on the server'; it means 'this code ships to and runs in the browser'. Because the boundary cascades to imports, you keep it as low (leaf-level) in the tree as possible so you don't accidentally pull large subtrees into the client bundle.

question: Which statement best describes The 'use client' boundary?
options: Adding 'use client' to the top of a module marks it — and every module it imports — as part of the client bundle. RSC pairs with Suspense so the server can send ready parts of the page first and stream slower sections as their data resolves, instead of blocking on the slowest query. Each Suspense boundary reveals independently with its own fallback, so above-the-fold content appears immediately while reviews or recommendations arrive later. This improves perceived performance without shipping extra client JS.

question: Which statement best describes Data fetching in RSC?
options: SSR runs your normal (client) components on the server to produce HTML for first paint, then ships their JS so the browser can hydrate them. RSC is about which components ship JS at all: server components emit a serialized payload, never send their code, and never hydrate. They are complementary — a framework can SSR the initial HTML while using RSC to keep non-interactive code off the client entirely.

Instead of plain HTML, server components are serialized into a compact RSC payload: a streamable description of the rendered tree with placeholders ('holes') marking where client components plug in. The client reads this payload to render the server-produced UI and then downloads and hydrates only the client islands. Monitoring payload size matters because it is transferred over the network on each request.

Server Actions let a client component invoke a server-side function (e.g., a mutation like add-to-cart) without bundling that logic into the browser. The action runs on the server with access to the database and secrets, and React wires up the call across the boundary. Always treat action arguments as untrusted input and validate/authorize inside the action, since anything callable from the client can be called with arbitrary data.
